questions.q: Why is setting `PasswordAuthentication no` in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` considered the single highest-value SSH hardening step?
options: It makes SSH connections faster
It prevents login via a stolen or guessed password entirely, requiring a trusted private key instead
It disables SSH completely for extra security
It only affects root login, not other accounts
questions.explain: With password authentication disabled, an attacker who guesses or steals a password still cannot log in — only possession of a matching private key allows authentication.

questions.q: After editing `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, why run `systemctl reload sshd` instead of `restart`?
options: reload is required because restart doesn't exist for sshd
reload applies the new configuration without dropping currently active SSH sessions
restart would delete the configuration file
There's no difference between the two commands
questions.explain: reload re-reads the configuration for a running service without terminating it, so existing connections (including the one you're using to make the change) stay alive — important since a mistake plus a restart could lock you out.

questions.q: When enabling `ufw` on a remote server you're connected to over SSH, why must you run `ufw allow 22/tcp` before `ufw enable`?
options: The order doesn't matter at all
Enabling the firewall with no explicit allow rule for your SSH port blocks your own connection immediately
ufw enable automatically allows port 22 by default
allow commands only work after the firewall is already enabled
questions.explain: ufw defaults to denying incoming traffic once enabled. Without an allow rule for SSH already in place, enabling it cuts off the very connection you're using to manage the server.

questions.q: In `firewalld`, what is the difference between a rule added with `--permanent` and one added without it?
options: There is no difference
A --permanent rule persists across reloads and reboots; a non-permanent rule only lasts until the next reload or reboot
--permanent rules apply only to IPv6 traffic
Non-permanent rules take priority over permanent ones
questions.explain: --permanent writes the rule to firewalld's persistent configuration so it survives a reload or reboot. Without it, the rule is only active in the current runtime configuration.

questions.q: Why is granting `sudo` access through group membership (e.g., adding a user to the `sudo` or `wheel` group) preferred over giving every person a shared root login?
options: Shared logins are actually more secure because fewer accounts exist
Group-based sudo access ties every privileged command to a specific person's identity, supporting accountability and least privilege
Group membership is the only way sudo can function at all
It has no real advantage over shared logins
questions.explain: Each person using their own named account with sudo privileges (via group membership) means privileged actions are logged against a real identity, rather than being indistinguishable actions under one shared root account.
